# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review

The treatment of coronary artery disease through percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has undergone several revolutionary phases, spanning balloon angioplasty, bare-metal stents, and drug-eluting stents (DES). While contemporary metallic DES have achieved excellent safety and efficacy, they introduce a permanent metallic "cage" that prevents physiological vasomotion, limits future surgical bypass options, and can trigger chronic inflammatory foreign-body responses leading to very late stent thrombosis. To overcome these limitations, the concept of a transient mechanical support—the bioresorbable vascular scaffold (BVS)—was introduced to provide temporary vessel scaffolding and drug elution before fully degrading into carbon dioxide and water, thereby allowing "vascular restorative therapy."

The clinical feasibility of this concept was initially established in first-in-human studies evaluating the everolimus-eluting, poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA)-based Absorb BVS (Abbott Vascular) [1]. These early, single-arm clinical cohorts demonstrated positive outcomes, with restored vasomotion and late luminal enlargement up to two years post-implantation [2]. On the basis of these promising initial data, the randomized, active-controlled ABSORB II trial was conducted, showing comparable acute success and one-year safety compared to metallic cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stents (CoCr-EES) [3]. However, as follow-up extended, three-year outcomes from ABSORB II revealed a higher incidence of target lesion failure (TLF) and scaffold thrombosis with the bioresorbable device [4]. Even after the expected timeframe for complete bioresorption, five-year follow-up of ABSORB II demonstrated persistent clinical risks, raising significant concerns [5].

To extensively validate the technology, several larger-scale, randomized trials were initiated. The pivotal, multicenter ABSORB III trial randomized 2,008 patients and established BVS non-inferiority to CoCr-EES at one year [6]. However, five-year clinical outcomes of ABSORB III demonstrated an elevated rate of TLF and device thrombosis before resorption was completed [7]. To evaluate BVS under strict, blinded conditions and optimized implantation techniques, the ABSORB IV trial was performed [8]. Unfortunately, despite these procedural improvements, the five-year results of ABSORB IV still showed a 3.0% absolute increase in TLF with BVS compared to CoCr-EES, although the risk period for device-related events stabilized after complete scaffold bioresorption at three years [9]. Mirroring these findings, other regional trials, including ABSORB Japan [10] and ABSORB China [11], reported acceptable short-term results but warned of late adverse signals. The AIDA trial, a large-scale investigator-initiated registry, confirmed a dramatically higher risk of device thrombosis, prompting early trial unblinding and recommending prolonged dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) [12].

Large patient-level meta-analyses further characterized these failures. Pooled data of the ABSORB clinical trials at one year [13] and two years [14] underscored the significantly elevated risk of device-oriented outcomes associated with BVS. Continued follow-up confirmed that the elevated risk persisted up to three years [15] and five years [16], demonstrating a clear time-varying safety profile that peaked during the intermediate degradation phase of the PLLA polymer.

The clinical failures of the first-generation Absorb BVS were primarily attributed to mechanical and procedural limitations. Analysis of scaffold thrombosis registries identified incomplete scaffold expansion, geographic mismatch, and abrupt polymer degradation as primary mechanical causes [17]. To optimize outcomes, clinical consensus recommended the "PSP" technique: aggressive pre-dilatation, precise scaffold sizing using quantitative coronary angiography or intravascular imaging, and mandatory post-dilatation with a non-compliant balloon [18]. High-resolution imaging studies using optical coherence tomography (OCT) and histopathology of scaffold thrombosis confirmed that the thick struts (~150 μm) of the first-generation BVS created local flow disruptions, delayed endothelialization, and provoked neoatherosclerosis within the degradation byproducts [19, 20].

In response to these findings, the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) and European Association of Percutaneous Cardiovascular Interventions (EAPCI) issued a task force report restricting BVS use to clinical trials [21], which was subsequently codified as a Class III (harmful) recommendation in clinical practice guidelines [22]. Despite these setbacks, specific clinical trials, such as the TROFI II trial in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction, suggested that when BVS was deployed with imaging guidance in expert hands, vascular healing and coronary physiology could be effectively restored [23].

To address the limitations of early polymer BVS, next-generation scaffolds have transitioned toward thinner struts and alternative materials. Bioresorbable metallic alloys, particularly magnesium-based scaffolds, were developed to provide higher radial strength with faster degradation profiles. The BIOSOLVE-I trial proved the initial feasibility of a drug-eluting absorbable metal scaffold [24]. This led to the development of the sirolimus-eluting Magmaris scaffold (Biotronik), which demonstrated stable clinical results and low late lumen loss at twelve months in the BIOSOLVE-II trial [25]. The long-term five-year follow-up of BIOSOLVE-II confirmed sustained safety with no very late scaffold thrombosis [26], a finding replicated in the larger, real-world BIOSOLVE-IV registry [27]. Concurrently, novel polymeric platforms were developed. The tyrosine polycarbonate-based Fantom scaffold (REVA Medical) offered thinner struts (~125 μm) and superior radiopacity, showing excellent six-month outcomes in the FANTOM II trial [28], which were maintained as safe and effective through long-term follow-up [29]. Furthermore, PLLA-based next-generation BVS, such as the MeRes100 scaffold with a strut thickness of 100 μm, demonstrated complete strut coverage and zero scaffold thrombosis in the MeRes-1 trial [30].

In conclusion, while first-generation BVS suffered from design flaws and high thrombosis rates, the field of bioresorbable scaffolds remains highly dynamic. Next-generation scaffolds with thinner struts (<120 μm) and refined degradation profiles, supported by routine intravascular imaging and optimized implantation protocols, are bridging the safety gap. Continued research is vital to realizing the ultimate goal of temporary mechanical support and complete vascular restoration in percutaneous coronary intervention.
